faq.q: What is the little glass bulb in a sprinkler?
faq.a: It is a sealed glass bulb holding a liquid that expands when heated. At a set temperature it bursts, releasing the plug so water can flow. The colour shows the temperature, with red meaning about 68 degrees.
asks: How does a sprinkler know there is a fire?

faq.q: Do all the sprinklers go off at once?
faq.a: No. Each head works on its own and only opens when the heat right above the fire bursts its bulb. In films they all go off together, but in real buildings usually only one or two open.
asks: Does one sprinkler set off the others?

faq.q: Can smoke set off a sprinkler?
faq.a: No. Sprinklers respond only to heat at the bulb. Smoke from burnt toast will set off a smoke alarm but not a sprinkler.
asks: Does burnt toast set off sprinklers?

faq.a: The deflector is the toothed metal plate under the head. The jet of water hits it and is broken into a wide umbrella of droplets that covers the floor below.
asks: Why does a sprinkler have a spiky plate?

faq.a: They start fighting a fire within minutes, right where it is, before it can spread, often putting it out before firefighters arrive.

facts: In standard glass-bulb sprinklers, a red bulb bursts at about 68 °C.
Each sprinkler head opens independently, so usually only those over the fire release water.
